newsitem.title: FRANCE: Croatia admitted to Council of Europe - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Croatia admitted to Council of Europe - diplomats.

text.p: The Council of Europe decided on Wednesday to admit Croatia as its 40th member after a six-month delay over human rights concerns, diplomats said.
The Balkan nation will officially become a member of the organisation -- which promotes democracy and human rights -- on November 6, they added.

Regarded as an antechamber to the European Union, the Strasbourg-based Council froze Croatia's application in May and set conditions concerning respect of the Dayton peace agreement on former Yugoslavia, democracy and press freedom.

"The only black spot is the Zagreb government's non-cooperation with the U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia. But that's a general problem which doesn't only concern Croatia," one diplomat said.

Wednesday's decision, taken by representatives of the body's Council of Ministers, reflects a majority view that Croatia has made sufficient progress to justify admission to the pan-European organisation, diplomats said.

Croatian Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa had on Tuesday expressed confidence that Croatia would be accepted following talks with European Commisssioner Hans van den Broek and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana.
Commission sources said van den Broek told Matesa he hoped EU member states that were also members of the council would admit Croatia provided the conditions had been met.
Diplomats said Germany, Croatia's main ally in the EU, had pressed strongly for Zagreb to be "rewarded for good behaviour."
In July, the Council formally invited Croatia to join but said entry would be delayed until it was satisfied President Franjo Tudjman had complied fully with the Dayton agreement.
In an unprecedented procedure, the Council reserved the right to reconsider its offer this month. But diplomats said no member state had spoken out against Croatia joining.
Since then, elections have been held successfully in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Croatia and rump Yugoslavia have also established diplomatic relations.
Progress has also been made on an amnesty law for Serbs who rebelled against Zagreb in 1991, the diplomats said.

On democracy and human rights, journalists charged with libelling the government have been acquitted and the country has adopted a new press law, although there are still concerns about minority rights and the Zagreb city council, they said.
In a report published in March, the Council's parliamentary assembly had raised issues including the status of independent media and of humanitarian organisations.
It added: "Membership of the Council is very widely seen as the best guarantee against violations of democratic rules and of violations of human rights."
Croatia will be the second former-Yugoslav republic to join the Council after Slovenia, which became a member in May 1993.
